Issued at 412 PM CDT Fri Sep 18 2026

Earlier fog over northern Missouri has eroded away this afternoon, 
with temperatures across the area climbing into the 90s as daytime 
heating has commenced. A warm frontal boundary draped across north-
central Missouri is projected to continue pushing northward through 
the rest of the afternoon, with agitated cumulus over central 
Missouri following upstream. While the presence of this cumulus 
suggests the presence of atmospheric instability, overall 
probabilities for showers and thunderstorms this afternoon and 
evening remain low, with greater synoptic forcing for ascent located 
further north with a surface cyclone and shortwave trough positioned 
over the Plains. 

This cyclone and associated shortwave will be the primary driver for 
storm chances overnight tonight. The greater focus for any severe 
activity resides closer to the immediate vicinity of the synoptic 
front/surface cyclone and forcing along the intensifying low-level 
jet. However, recent CAM guidance continues to indicate additional 
convection popping up along a boundary that ejects off the primary 
line towards the southeast, bringing higher chances (30-45%) of 
precipitation to an area generally along/northwest of I-35 by early 
morning tomorrow. The overall environment doesn't look incredibly 
favorable for the development of severe storms with this activity, 
with decreasing instability in the mixed-layer and marginal shear as 
the night progresses. However, stronger storms with heavy rainfall 
and lightning remain possible.

By tomorrow morning, activity looks to taper off across northern 
Missouri with the retreating low-level jet and shortwave trough 
towards the Great Lakes. However, another shortwave trough will 
reinvigorate the atmosphere for a renewed chance for showers and 
thunderstorms in the evening/overnight via enhanced warm/moist 
transport across the forecast area as the shortwave lifts northeast 
across Missouri. This, coupled with the synoptic-scale cold front 
lingering behind the previous system pushing southeastward, will 
provide ample instability and ascent for the development of 
strong/severe storms. However, shear looks to remain just marginal 
(~25-30 kts) alongside mid-level lapse rates around 6.5-7 degC/km, 
which brings into question the ability of storm updrafts to organize 
and maintain intensity. With these factors in mind, still 
anticipating a severe hail/wind threat with any storms that are able 
to organize and maintain intensity, but confidence in widespread 
severe storms is not high. Another caveat to consider with activity 
tomorrow is the potential for heavy rainfall to create some 
hydrological concerns. Some guidance indicates that thunderstorms 
could train along the boundary with parallel moisture transport 
vectors in the low-levels, which, coupled with climatologically high 
PWATs around 2 inches, enhances efficient/prolonged rainfall in 
storms for some risk of flooding. However, other guidance suggests 
that rainfall will be progressive enough that these concerns might 
be mitigated. 

Activity on Saturday will influence how Sunday pans out, 
specifically regarding the potential for continued showers/storms to 
close out the weekend. The cold front looks to continue pushing 
southward, with guidance indicating increasing chances for 
precipitation (30-60%) Sunday afternoon and evening along this 
boundary. PoPs will be bolstered by a passing low-level shortwave in 
the flow providing greater synoptic ascent with enhanced vorticity 
advection. However, there is continued spread in the position of the 
cold front and how fast it progresses southward during Sunday. If it 
passes through quicker, the environment looks to be less favorable 
for activity with greater cool/dry advection from the north. This 
trend will need to continue to be monitored in subsequent forecasts 
to better hone messaging closer to the end of the weekend.

Going into the week next week, PoPs decrease as weather cools 
and dry considerably from this previous week under
north/northeasterly flow, ushering in much cooler (and better) 
weather relative to this prior week. High temperatures reside 
in the 60s and 70s for much of the area through the early week, 
with overnight lows dipping into the 50s. By midweek, there is 
indication of a renewed ridge building across the central CONUS,
which will serve to increase temperatures once again by the end
of the forecast period across the area. However, this rise in 
temperatures looks to not be as dramatic, with highs topping out
in the high 70s along and south of I-70.
